claim: School-level AI essay policy is genuinely CONTESTED across the sector, and the dominant reality (2024-2026) is the ABSENCE of policy. Kaplan's July-August 2025 survey of 220 admissions officers found that on using GenAI to WRITE the essay, only 2% of colleges have an official policy ALLOWING it, 30% have a policy BANNING it, and 68% have NO policy at all; on brainstorming, 27% allow / 4% ban / 69% no policy; on feedback, 21% allow / 5% ban / 73% no policy. The minority of schools that DO have policies span the full range: blanket ban (Brown, Georgetown), detailed permit-with-limits (Caltech, Yale, Cornell, Vanderbilt, CMU, WashU, Emory, UVA), and brief Common-App-echo. Officer sentiment skews negative: 50% unfavorable toward GenAI in essays, 26% neutral, only 14% favorable.

application.content: Never assume a target school's silence means permission. For each school on a student's list, check that school's own admissions/application-policy page that cycle; if it has no AI statement (the 68% case), default to the Common App fraud baseline (no AI-authored substance) AND the strictest policy among the student's OTHER schools. Build the student's process to satisfy the strictest list-member, since one essay (e.g. the Common App personal statement) is sent to all of them. The variance itself is the actionable insight: there is no single 'is AI allowed' answer to give a student -- the answer is per-school and changes yearly.

sources.citation: Kaplan Survey: Colleges Clarify Rules on AI Use in Admissions Essays (220 admissions officers, July-Aug 2025)
sources.authorRole: Kaplan (named survey of 220 admissions officers, established education company)

sources.citation: AI Use in College Essays: What Top 30 Admissions Offices Will (and Won't) Allow | College Essay Advisors
sources.authorRole: College Essay Advisors (named admissions-essay consultancy, top-30 policy roundup)

positions: No policy / silence (majority, ~68% of colleges per Kaplan) -- applicant left to infer rules; Common App baseline applies by default.
Permit-with-limits (e.g. Caltech, Yale, Cornell, Vanderbilt, CMU, WashU, Emory, UVA) -- AI OK for grammar + brainstorming, banned for drafting/substance.
Strict ban (Brown 'under any circumstances except proofreading'; Georgetown) -- no AI in application content at all.
Sentiment: most admissions officers are personally unfavorable (50%) toward GenAI in essays even where no policy exists.
whoHoldsWhat: Kaplan 2025 survey holds: 2% allow-writing policy / 30% ban-writing / 68% none.
Caltech & Yale hold: brainstorming + grammar permitted, substance prohibited (detailed guidance).
Brown & Georgetown hold: AI not permitted under any circumstances (proofreading-only carve-out at Brown).
Common App holds: AI 'substantive content or output' submitted as own work = fraud (binding default for 1,000+ members).
College Essay Advisors (2025 roundup) holds: ~7% ban / 27% limited-use / 70% no policy among top-30 -- broadly consistent with Kaplan.

connections.note: The Common App baseline is what governs the 68% of schools with no policy of their own.
Brown/Georgetown are the strict-ban anchor of this spectrum.
Caltech/Yale are the detailed-permit anchor of this spectrum.

provenanceTrail: Kaplan press release (220 AOs, July-Aug 2025) fetched 2026-06-18 with exact splits (write 2/30/68; brainstorm 27/4/69; feedback 21/5/73; sentiment 50/26/14). College Essay Advisors top-30 roundup (2025) gives a broadly agreeing independent breakdown (~7% ban, 27% limited, 70% none) -- two independent Tier-2 sources agreeing on the SHAPE of the distribution, which is why this clears the bar as CONTESTED-with-sources rather than provisional. Named-school positions cross-checked against Tier-1 policy pages in entries 002/003/005. Note one freshness discrepancy: College Essay Advisors classified Yale as 'no policy' while Yale's own page (entry 002) has one -- resolved toward the Tier-1 school page. Flagged volatile: the percentages will move every cycle as more schools publish policies.
